name: sand
prompt: Use your image generation tool. The attached image is a reference: warm sand ground, 16x16 pixels, from our top-down pixel-art game, shown enlarged on magenta. Generate a NEW image of the same warm sand ground - same design, same colors, same top-down three-quarter view - redrawn as pixel art 64 pixels wide and 64 pixels tall, far more pixels than the reference, with fine warm sand seen from above: soft low ripples drawn as short broken dashes, scattered grains, a few tiny pale and dark pebbles, gentle bands of lighter and deeper tan. It wraps: whatever leaves the right edge comes back in at the same row on the left edge and whatever leaves the bottom comes back in at the top, so the colours and shapes along opposite edges match exactly and nothing is cut at an edge. No single object, light spot or dark clump stands out, so that a field of copies shows no repeat. Light from the upper left, shown only as a gentle hue shift (warm lights, cool darks) in the texture, no cast shadows and no outline.. Every pixel stays a crisp square of one flat color, no anti-aliasing, each one about 1/64 of the drawing's width: draw no smaller pixels than that. No outline: it is a ground texture that fills the whole 64x64 square edge to edge, centered on the magenta. Its left edge continues its right edge and its top continues its bottom, so it repeats without a seam. Painterly pixel art: every surface shifts hue as it turns from light to shadow (warm lights, cool darks), with ambient light and colour bounced from neighbouring parts, visible material texture (wood grain, stone pores, cloth weave) drawn in pixels, and an outline whose colour follows the surface it borders rather than one flat dark line. Rich colour, as many shades as the object needs. Solid flat pure magenta #FF00FF background around it, no text, no shadow, no extra objects. The other attached images show the drawing style to match: the same shading depth, hue shifts, texture and outline treatment. The 64x64 drawing fills most of the image. Do not process the image with code afterwards; just generate it and save it as sand.png in the current directory.
